topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: Micron 3-DOF system design and bench characterisation
citation: MacLachlan RA, Becker BC, Cuevas Tabarés J, Podnar GW, Lobes LA Jr, Riviere CN. Micron: an actively stabilized handheld tool for microsurgery. IEEE Trans Robot. 2012;28(1):195-212.
task_or_setup: 3-DOF parallel piezo manipulator in a 40 g handpiece moves a ~40 mm tool tip relative to the handle; 2 kHz optical PSD tracker (ASAP) measures handle and tip pose in world frame; Internal Model Control position servo at 2 kHz in link-length space with charge-controlled piezo drive; frequency/step responses obtained by injecting simulated handle motion numerically into the running loop; servo tracking error measured against a pre-recorded tremor disturbance
participants_or_bench: Bench/system identification; no human subjects for these numbers
comparator: Two controller tunings (critically damped vs underdamped); theoretical 'delay-only' canceller with the same 3 ms delay
key_quantitative_findings: Actuators: six Thunder TH-10R laminated piezo bending actuators (2 in series per leg x 3 legs), -240 to +480 V, 4 mA peak; force >1 N; slew rate >100 mm/s; tip workspace extent ~2 mm but largest enclosed cube ~400 um per side; actuator travel +/-400 um; kinematic calibration error 40 um RMS. Sensing: 2 kS/s pose, 4 um resolution (abstract); LED noise 0.74 um RMS (1 kHz bandwidth); tip noise 5.7 um RMS (full bandwidth), 1.8 um RMS (100 Hz bandwidth); 4 cm tracking workspace. Loop: identified pure delay 2 ms; nominal delay 8 cycles = 4 ms incl. inverse filter; closed-loop servo bandwidth 84 Hz (critically damped, phase margin 64 deg) to 123 Hz (underdamped, PM 42 deg, 5 dB peaking); first lateral resonance ~150 Hz, ~400 Hz resonance depends on tip mass. Performance: hand-motion attenuation >=15 dB (fivefold); 3D servo tracking error vs pre-recorded tremor 4.8 um RMS / 41 um max (underdamped) and 6.1 um RMS / 62 um max (critically damped); induced tip noise 1.6 / 1.2 um RMS; 200 um handle step gives 70 um overshoot (underdamped). Authors: in the <30 Hz band the servo is a pure delay, so rejection can only improve by reducing delay or predicting the disturbance.
units_and_conditions: Tip position in world frame from the same optical tracker (induced noise measured with a fibre-optic displacement sensor); RMS and maximum as labelled; 'bandwidth' = closed-loop position-servo bandwidth, not tremor band; physiological tremor; tip in free space (no contact load); attenuation declines above ~4 Hz because of delay
locator: Author manuscript: Abstract p1; Sec II.B p5 and Fig. 10 (actuator, force, slew, workspace, 40 g); Sec II.D p6 (tracker noise); Sec II.H p8 (+/-400 um, 40 um RMS); Sec II.J p8 (2 ms delay); Sec II.K.3 p11 and Table III (4 ms, 100/200 Hz tunings); Sec II.N p11-12, Table IV, Figs 23-26 (84/123 Hz, PM, tracking error, noise, step)
limitations: Handle-motion responses synthesised numerically (no physical shaker); reference sensing is an external line-of-sight optical tracker; 50 mm housing diameter and high-voltage drive; poorly damped resonances cap bandwidth; authors state suppression is delay-limited
relevance_to_design: Reference architecture for world-referenced closed-loop tip stabilisation; quantifies what ~2-4 ms loop delay and ~100 Hz servo bandwidth buy (>=15 dB) and shows the residual is set by delay
transferability_reason: Servo/IMC and saturation-management principles transfer and the +/-0.2-0.4 mm travel is similar to our +/-0.5 mm; but the world reference is an external 2 kHz optical tracker a pen cannot carry, the tip never touches a surface (mN or zero load vs 0.2-2 N), and -240/+480 V drive and 50 mm housing are not pen-compatible
design_implication: Budget total sensing-to-nib delay at <=3-5 ms if >=10-15 dB rejection at 8-10 Hz is required; target >=80-100 Hz closed-loop nib bandwidth with first resonance >=150 Hz; copy Micron's saturation handling (filter cut-off raised from 50% travel, alternate-goal substitution)

lead_verification: re-verified by lead against author manuscript PDF 2026-09-27 (84-123 Hz bandwidth, +/-400 um travel, 15 dB)

topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: Micron 3-DOF human-in-the-loop evaluation
citation: MacLachlan RA, Becker BC, Cuevas Tabarés J, Podnar GW, Lobes LA Jr, Riviere CN. Micron: an actively stabilized handheld tool for microsurgery. IEEE Trans Robot. 2012;28(1):195-212.
task_or_setup: Hold still 30 s; trace a 500 um circle for 60 s; move 600 um and hold 15 s (x4); tip kept just above a laser-engraved rubber target (no contact); 27 G needle (400 um shaft); 29x stereo microscope with oblique-light shadow cue; conditions: off, low-pass goal filter (1.5 Hz), 'scaling' shelving filter (fL 0.15 Hz, fH 2 Hz, gain 1/3), both with 1 mm/s goal-velocity limiter; nested Latin square; 6 sessions per subject, sessions 4-6 analysed; logged at 200 Hz; not blinded
participants_or_bench: 6 humans: 3 ophthalmic surgeons, 3 novices (healthy, physiological tremor)
key_quantitative_findings: Scaling vs off: 3D max error 291 -> 157 um (-46%), 2D max 219 -> 105 um (-52%), 3D RMS 85 -> 58 um (-32%). Low-pass vs off: 3D max 229 um (-21%), 2D max 164 um (-25%), 3D RMS 77 um (-10%). Move time 2.9 s (off) -> 3.5 s (low-pass, +18%) -> 4.0 s (scaling, +37%). Handle (hand) motion rose 87.1 -> 117.6 um with scaling (+35%, significant). Hold-still 3D max motion -44% at tip and -30% at the sclerotomy. Normal microsurgical tremor is 'several hundred microns peak-to-peak'; eye-hand loop critical frequency 0.5-2 Hz; low-pass corner below ~1 Hz felt 'bouncy' and near-unusable at 0.5 Hz; 90% of tip speeds <2 mm/s; 1 mm/s exceeded 30% of the time.
units_and_conditions: Error = tip position relative to target from optical tracker, pooled across tasks; 3D/2D maximum and 3D RMS as labelled; physiological tremor under 29x magnification; free space
locator: Author manuscript: Abstract; Sec I.A-B p1-2 and Figs 1-3 (tremor, eye-hand loop, speed CDF); Sec II.F p7 and Table II (filters); Sec III.A p13; Table VI p14 (error metrics); Table VII p15 (move time, hand motion); Sec III.B.2 p14 (sclerotomy); Sec IV p16
limitations: Healthy physiological tremor only; no tip contact; unblinded; earlier controller version; n=6; slow visually guided microsurgical motions
relevance_to_design: Net human-in-the-loop benefit (10-52% error reduction) is much smaller than bench handle-to-tip attenuation (>=15 dB) because users slow down and move the handle more when loop gain is reduced
transferability_reason: Human adaptation effects (slowing, larger handle motion) are likely to recur in writing; but goal filters were tuned for slow visually guided microsurgery (1.5 Hz corner, 1 mm/s limiter) and would erase handwriting strokes; no pathological tremor; no paper contact
design_implication: Judge the pen on humans writing, reporting writing speed and handle motion as well as trace error; do not copy Micron's low-pass/scaling goal filters; tremor-band (adaptive notch/predictive) cancellation that passes voluntary strokes is required

topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: 6-DOF Micron with piezo ultrasonic linear motors and side-load tolerance
citation: Yang S, MacLachlan RA, Riviere CN. Manipulator design and operation of a six-degree-of-freedom handheld tremor-canceling microsurgical instrument. IEEE/ASME Trans Mechatron. 2015;20(2).
task_or_setup: Gough-Stewart platform driven by six SQUIGGLE SQL-RV-1.8 piezo ultrasonic lead-screw motors; PID in link-length space with fifth-order duty-cycle linearisation; clamped tests: +/-2 mm sinusoids at 1-5 mm/s; side loads 0-0.3 N applied at a remote centre of motion 30 mm above the tool mount while tracking +/-1 mm at 1 mm/s; handheld pointing task 20 s at 25x with a fixed goal (all motion rejected); automated circle tracing 1-4 mm diameter
participants_or_bench: Bench (clamped) + 1 subject without surgical training for handheld tasks (5 trials)
key_quantitative_findings: Motors 2.8x2.8x6 mm, stall >0.3 N at 3.3 V (+/-0.5 N assumed in simulation); motor stroke 5.3 mm; tip workspace cylinder 4 mm dia x 4 mm; manipulator 23 mm dia x 37 mm, 14.4 g (moving parts 2.3 g); instrument 28.5 mm dia x 126 mm, 70 g; design side load 0.2 N (scleral entry). Optical tracker 1 kHz, <10 um RMS noise, 27 cm3. RMS tracking error vs side load (1 mm/s): 6, 6, 10, 15, 17, 17, 47 um at 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30 N; 0.15 N tolerated over whole workspace. Clamped RMS error 6-11 um at 1 mm/s, 7-22 um at 2 mm/s, 9-43 um at 5 mm/s. Handheld pointing: RMS 112+/-8 -> 12+/-2 um (89.3%), max 361 -> 49 um. Automated circles 10-20 um RMS (>20 um at 4 mm, 5 mm/s) vs manual 105-140 um. Cancelling 'currently limited by a chattering instability in the range of 50-100 Hz'; closed-loop bandwidth and latency not stated.
units_and_conditions: Tip position error from optical tracker, RMS and max; lateral side load applied at the RCM on the shaft, not a normal load at the tip; free space; pointing used a fixed goal (no voluntary motion passed)
locator: Abstract; Table I (spec); Sec II-III (motor, stroke 5.3 mm, 0.2 N design load, Fig. 3); Sec IV (control, linearisation, Fig. 8); Sec V.A Table II (side load); Sec V.B Table III; Sec V.C and Fig. 10-11 (handheld); Sec VI (chattering 50-100 Hz)
limitations: Handheld data n=1; fixed-goal pointing overstates benefit for tasks with voluntary motion; stick-slip ultrasonic motors caused chattering; loads applied laterally at the RCM; external tracker
relevance_to_design: Only handheld tremor canceller with quantified lateral-load tolerance in the 0.1-0.3 N range, i.e. the low end of plausible nib friction loads
transferability_reason: mm-scale travel, 70 g mass and ~0.25 N load tolerance are pen-relevant, but error rose to 47 um at 0.30 N, stick-slip motors limited bandwidth (chattering 50-100 Hz), the load is not a frictional tip contact, and sensing is external
design_implication: Size nib actuators for >=2-3x the worst-case lateral friction at 2 N normal load and measure error-vs-lateral-load curves like Table II; treat stick-slip (inertial/ultrasonic) actuators as high-risk for 4-12 Hz cancellation

topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: 6-DOF Micron handheld performance when voluntary motion must be preserved
citation: Yang S, Wells TS, MacLachlan RA, Riviere CN. Performance of a 6-degree-of-freedom active microsurgical manipulator in handheld tasks. Conf Proc IEEE Eng Med Biol Soc (EMBC). 2013.
task_or_setup: 6-DOF Micron; hold still 20 s above a rubber target; trace a 500 um circle for 20 s; eye-phantom hold with RCM constraint; goal filters: low-pass (1.5 Hz corner, high attenuation beyond 10 Hz) and motion scaling (unity gain <0.15 Hz, ~1/3 from 0.15-2 Hz) vs unaided; 5 trials per task/mode; surgical microscope
participants_or_bench: Number of participants not explicitly stated (text refers to 'a participant')
key_quantitative_findings: Hold still (rubber target): 3D RMS 93 um unaided -> 61 um low-pass -> 40 um scaling; max 301 -> 192 -> 103 um (scaling max = 34% of unaided, p=0.003). Circle tracing: unaided 86 um RMS / 244 um max; max error 70% (low-pass) and 51% (scaling, p=0.02) of unaided. Control bandwidth limited by chattering instability at 50-100 Hz.

topic: Micron in tissue contact: hybrid position/force control (tip loads handled by active handheld tools)
citation: Wells TS, Yang S, MacLachlan RA, Lobes LA Jr, Martel JN, Riviere CN. Hybrid position/force control of an active handheld micromanipulator for membrane peeling. Int J Med Robot Comput Assist Surg. 2016.
task_or_setup: Membrane peeling on PDMS phantom and chicken-egg inner shell membrane with 6-DOF Micron plus 2-DOF fibre-Bragg-grating force-sensing tool; position loop with 1.5 Hz low-pass goal; force PID at 1 kHz engaged above threshold; soft/hard force limits 2/4 mN (phantom) and 2/6 mN (egg); 16x microscope
comparator: Micron position control (tremor cancellation) without force loop
key_quantitative_findings: FBG sensor 0.25 mN resolution, 2 kHz, 0.71 mm diameter. Phantom: RMS force -32% (x) / -41% (y), max force -46% / -63%; position-control max 7.5+/-2.7 mN (x), 10.0+/-3.5 mN (y). Egg membrane: RMS -34% / -36%, max -54% / -58%; max 15.7+/-5.5 -> 7.2+/-1.4 mN (x), 12.5+/-5.3 -> 5.2+/-1.3 mN (y). Duration unchanged (p=0.57, 0.72); tears 1.4+/-1.4 vs 0.8+/-1.1 (n.s.). No friction or stick-slip analysis.
units_and_conditions: Lateral tool-tip contact forces in mN on soft membranes
locator: Methods (sensor, controller gains, constraints); Results (force tables/figures)
limitations: Contact forces 2-16 mN on compliant tissue; no rigid-surface friction; small n
relevance_to_design: Highest-load contact use of an active handheld stabiliser located: still ~100x below nib loads
transferability_reason: Forces (<=16 mN) and soft tissue are one to three orders of magnitude below 0.2-2 N frictional nib contact on paper; no evidence on stability of a position servo against Coulomb friction
design_implication: Assume nothing about Micron-style servo stability in frictional contact; develop and test a friction-aware position/impedance controller with nib normal-load sensing from scratch

topic: Causal tremor estimation: Kalman-filter state estimation with velocity feedforward in Micron
citation: Becker BC, MacLachlan RA, Riviere CN. State estimation and feedforward tremor suppression for a handheld micromanipulator with a Kalman filter. Proc IEEE/RSJ Int Conf Intell Robots Syst (IROS). 2011:5160-5165.
task_or_setup: 3-DOF Micron hold-still at a fixed 3D set point; PID feedback vs feedback + feedforward of Kalman-estimated handle velocity (u = u_FB + alpha*u_FF); controllers switched at random every 5 s without informing the operator; ground truth = tip position through 100 Hz zero-lag 2nd-order Butterworth; chirp 1 Hz-1 kHz injected into pose for frequency response; clamped-in-vise baseline
participants_or_bench: 1 operator familiar with Micron, no surgical experience
comparator: PID feedback only; clamped (no tremor) floor
key_quantitative_findings: Model: linear KF, constant-acceleration model (position, velocity, acceleration) per translational axis and constant-angular-velocity per Euler angle = 15 states; separate KFs for tip and handle; actuator input rotated into world frame in the tip filter; run at 2 kHz on ASAP data (2 kHz, <10 um RMS). Delay compensation: no explicit multi-step predictor; feedforward of estimated handle velocity anticipates disturbance during actuation latency. RMS tip error 7.9 um (feedback) -> 3.4 um (feedback+feedforward) = -56.7%; clamped floor 1.4 um; about -7 dB additional attenuation at 10 Hz; error spectrum rises near 60 Hz (Bode integral); 10-20 um tremor disturbances reduced to 5-10 um.
units_and_conditions: 3D tip position error vs set point, RMS (um); physiological tremor; free space; Micron range quoted as 2x2x1 mm
locator: Sec II.C (ASAP); Sec III.A eqs (10)-(13) (KF); Sec III.B eqs (14)-(18) (feedforward); Sec IV.B-C; Table I; Figs 4-6
limitations: n=1; hold-still only (no voluntary motion); relies on world-frame optical tracking; hand-set covariances
relevance_to_design: Shows a lightweight model-based estimator can halve residual error when the servo is latency-limited
transferability_reason: A 15-state linear KF with velocity feedforward is sensor-agnostic and cheap enough for a pen MCU with IMU and nib-position sensing; the only non-transferable part is the external world reference
design_implication: Build disturbance-velocity feedforward from a state estimator into the nib controller from the start and A/B it against pure feedback on the pen bench using identical tremor playback

topic: Inertial-only handheld canceller: first Micron prototype (IMU + open-loop piezo stacks + WFLC)
citation: Riviere CN, Ang WT, Khosla PK. Toward active tremor canceling in handheld microsurgical instruments. IEEE Trans Robot Autom. 2003;19(5):793-800.
task_or_setup: Pen-sized instrument with all-accelerometer 6-DOF inertial sensing, WFLC-based estimation at 1 kHz, open-loop 3-DOF parallel piezo-stack manipulator; mounted on a cam-driven oscillating plate (~9 Hz); tip tracked with ASAP
key_quantitative_findings: Prototype 170 g, 210 mm long, 22 mm mean diameter (second prototype 130 mm, 19 mm, 100 g). Actuators: TS18-H5-202 stacks (5x5x18 mm, ~14.5 um at 100 V, 50 us response, up to 840 N), 7 per actuator -> >=100 um per axis; manipulator trajectory tracking 2.5 um (1-D) and 11.2 um (3-D) RMS. Cancellation at ~9 Hz: 1-D axial 51 -> 25 um p-p (-51%); 3-D vector 91 -> 60 um p-p (-34%). Accuracy limited to ~30 um p-p 'largely due to sensing inaccuracies'; noise increased at other frequencies.
units_and_conditions: Equivalent peak-to-peak = RMS x 2*sqrt(2); tip displacement; sinusoidal bench motion; free space; open loop (no manipulator position sensing)
locator: Sec IV.A (hardware, Table I); Sec IV.B-C (testbed, results, Table II, Figs 10-12); Sec V (noise floor, second prototype)
limitations: Bench sinusoid only; open loop; later abandoned because inertial sensing could not cancel low-frequency motion (ACT-01 Sec I.D)

transferability_reason: Size and sensing match a pen, but results are free-space bench sinusoids and the IMU noise/drift floor (~30 um p-p) limits what can be cancelled; no contact loads
design_implication: With IMU-only sensing restrict cancellation to the tremor band, characterise the IMU noise floor at the nib, and add nib-to-housing position sensing so the actuator is not run open loop

topic: Causal tremor estimation: WFLC/FLC adaptive canceller (bench cantilever)
citation: Riviere CN, Rader RS, Thakor NV. Adaptive canceling of physiological tremor for improved precision in microsurgery. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 1998;45(7):839-846.
task_or_setup: 1-D stainless cantilever (28 mm) whose base is moved by a voice coil replaying recorded surgeon hand motion; two piezo elements (12.7x18.3x0.19 mm) at the base cancel; Hall-effect sensor at the tip; WFLC with 6th-order elliptic 7-13 Hz band-pass pre-filter estimates tremor frequency; FLC without pre-filter generates the cancelling command; 1 kHz sampling; 15 s tests
participants_or_bench: Bench; 25 unfiltered hand-motion recordings from 5 experienced eye surgeons (simulated vitreoretinal surgery) plus synthetic signals
comparator: Uncompensated beam; offline zero-phase 2.25 Hz low-pass 'voluntary' estimate
key_quantitative_findings: 10 Hz sinusoid (~12 um p-p): -71.8% RMS; 8.5-11.5 Hz modulated sine: -63.1%; high-passed tremor: -40.6+/-8.6%; 25 raw recordings: 6-16 Hz band RMS 2.2 -> 0.8 um (-66.9+/-15.6%, p<0.01) and RMSE vs voluntary estimate 5.1 -> 3.4 um (-30.4+/-14.0%). Phase: cancelling FLC path is 'zero-phase'; pre-filter lag affects only the frequency estimate (stated negligible). Hall sensor noise ~2 um p-p; beam resonance ~312 Hz excited; loading by tissue contact 'not dealt with'.
units_and_conditions: Beam-tip displacement (Hall sensor), RMS in um; physiological tremor of a few um; 1 kHz; free space
locator: Abstract; Sec II.A (WFLC, pre-filter); Sec II.B-C (bench, 1 kHz); Sec III, Tables I-II; Sec IV (sensor noise, 312 Hz, contact caveat)
limitations: 1-D bench; um-scale physiological tremor; ideal tip sensing; single-dominant-frequency model; no contact
relevance_to_design: Foundational MCU-cheap causal quasi-periodic canceller with near-zero in-band phase
transferability_reason: Algorithm ports directly to a pen MCU, but amplitudes, single-frequency assumption and free-space bench differ from multi-frequency non-stationary ET/PD tremor during writing (see ACT-09, ACT-14)
design_implication: Implement WFLC/FLC as the causal baseline, test with recorded pathological writing tremor at up to +/-0.5 mm, and report tremor-band and whole-trajectory error separately as done here

topic: Causal tremor estimation: BMFLC vs WFLC (+RLS/Kalman variants) and voluntary-motion separation delay
citation: Veluvolu KC, Ang WT. Estimation of physiological tremor from accelerometers for real-time applications. Sensors. 2011;11(3):3020-3036.
task_or_setup: Offline one-step-ahead (k+1) estimation on recorded tremor with WFLC, WFLC-Kalman, BMFLC-LMS, BMFLC-RLS, BMFLC-Kalman (band 7-14 Hz, frequency spacing 0.1); pointing and tracing tasks recorded with optical M2S2 (0.7 um resolution, 250 Hz), wrist rested; test data zero-phase band-pass filtered 6-14 Hz before estimation 'for sake of ideal comparison'; separate voluntary/tremor separation on raw data
participants_or_bench: 6 microsurgeons + 6 novice subjects, 2 trials per task
comparator: WFLC, WFLC-Kalman, BMFLC-LMS; causal and zero-phase 2 Hz low-pass for voluntary separation
key_quantitative_findings: Estimation accuracy (surgeon #1 example): WFLC 90%, WFLC-Kalman 93%, BMFLC 94%, BMFLC-RLS 99%, BMFLC-Kalman 99.5%. Mean RMS error, surgeons: WFLC 0.956+/-0.441, WFLC-KF 0.632+/-0.263, BMFLC 0.408+/-0.201, BMFLC-RLS 0.076+/-0.051, BMFLC-KF 0.003+/-0.002 um (novices similar). Voluntary separation on raw data: BMFLC delay 0.082 s (RMSE 4.61 um) vs causal 2 Hz low-pass 0.2 s (17.8 um); surgeon example 0.072 s (6.63 um) vs 0.186 s (26.5 um). Authors: real-time band-pass pre-filtering 'causes delay and it decreases the accuracy'; tremor showed multiple dominant frequencies in 7-11 Hz (2-5 Hz wide).
units_and_conditions: Tip displacement (um) from optical sensor; one-step prediction at 250 Hz (4 ms); physiological tremor; offline
locator: Sec 2 (data, M2S2); Sec 4 (Figs 5-6 delays; parameters; Fig. 7 accuracies); Table 1 (RMSE)
limitations: Non-causal zero-phase pre-filtering of test data and a 4 ms horizon make accuracies optimistic; physiological, not pathological, tremor; offline
relevance_to_design: Shows multi-frequency Fourier banks beat single-frequency WFLC and quantifies the tens-of-ms cost of causal voluntary/tremor separation
transferability_reason: BMFLC-Kalman is MCU-friendly and suits IMU data in a pen, but headline accuracies come from idealised non-causal pre-filtering and would not survive a causal pipeline with real pen latency
design_implication: Adopt BMFLC-Kalman as a baseline but evaluate all estimators on raw, causally processed pen data at the measured loop delay; budget tens of ms for any explicit voluntary/tremor separation unless a predictor covers it

topic: Causal tremor estimation: unavoidable phase delay and multi-step prediction
citation: Veluvolu KC, Tatinati S, Hong SM, Ang WT. Multi-step prediction of physiological tremor for robotics applications. Conf Proc IEEE Eng Med Biol Soc (EMBC). 2013. Journal version: Multistep prediction of physiological tremor for surgical robotics applications. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 2013.

topic: Learned tremor estimation: PHTNet deep bidirectional GRU (pathological tremor)
citation: Shahtalebi S, Atashzar SF, Samotus O, Patel RV, Jog MS, Mohammadi A. PHTNet: characterization and deep mining of involuntary pathological hand tremor using recurrent neural network models. Sci Rep. 2020;10:2195.
task_or_setup: 4-layer bidirectional GRU (400 hidden features), 4 s input windows at 100 Hz, trained to output the voluntary component one sample ahead; training/test targets built by adding synthesised voluntary sinusoids (amplitude U(0,0.25), frequency U(0,3) Hz, random phase) to recorded rest/postural tremor
participants_or_bench: 81 PD and ET patients, 250 assessments, 87.5 h; Noraxon 3-axis accelerometer on the dorsum of the hand at 1500 Hz, down-sampled to 100 Hz
key_quantitative_findings: MSE (test) 0.00104 per segment; 0.00049 for the last sample (forward cells, online use); validation 0.00111. Normalised-MSE improvement vs BMFLC / E-BMFLC / WAKE: +89.58% / +89.01% / +91.07% (test), +88.42% / +87.78% / +90.18% (validation), p=5.96E-08. Horizon one sample = 10 ms. Output power above 3 Hz strongly reduced. Inference latency, parameter count and hardware not reported; authors note it needs 'relatively stronger computational support' (cloud approach proposed).
units_and_conditions: Accelerometer-derived hand motion in normalised units; MSE on synthesised voluntary component; offline
locator: Methods (dataset, data preparation, architecture); Table 2 (MSE); Table 3 (improvements); Discussion (compute)
limitations: Semi-synthetic ground truth (voluntary = random sinusoids <=3 Hz); one-step horizon; offline; backward (bidirectional) cells unusable online; compute unreported; Ibrahim et al. 2021 state it needs 100-150 ms before it estimates properly (secondary claim)
relevance_to_design: Largest pathological-tremor dataset; shows learned models beat Fourier-type estimators on this benchmark
transferability_reason: Voluntary motion modelled as <=3 Hz sinusoids does not represent handwriting strokes; 10 ms horizon is shorter than realistic pen latency; likely too large for a pen MCU; no hardware loop
design_implication: Do not adopt without re-benchmarking on causal pen/handwriting data at the measured delay; useful as an offline teacher or for dataset characterisation

topic: Causal tremor estimation: WAKE wavelet + adaptive Kalman one-step predictor

task_or_setup: Real-time tremor prediction scheme (wavelet decomposition of the last 2^J samples, J=5, plus adaptive Kalman/AR model, Yule-Walker order p=17) predicts one sample ahead; hyper-parameter adaptation on 5 s windows; offline evaluation on synthetic data (10 signals, 100 Hz, tremor 6-14 Hz), Motus gyroscope data and a smartphone-accelerometer PD dataset

key_quantitative_findings: Motus dataset NRMSE (mean of 5): BMFLC 0.1046, E-BMFLC 0.0741, WAKE 0.0437; window L=5 s chosen (minimum NRMSE 0.0378 at L=9 s); horizon one sample (10 ms at 100 Hz); no latency or compute figures.

topic: Learned multi-step voluntary-motion prediction vs WFLC in a closed-loop bench (Parkinsonian tremor)
citation: Ibrahim A, Zhou Y, Jenkins ME, Trejos AL, Naish MD. Real-time voluntary motion prediction and Parkinson's tremor reduction using deep neural networks. IEEE Trans Neural Syst Rehabil Eng. 2021;29:1413-1423.
task_or_setup: 1D-CNN-MLP (2 CNN layers x 64 filters + 1 MLP layer) on IMU angular velocity predicts voluntary motion 10-100 steps ahead; bench: two coupled Maxon EC-max 16 motors (29:1), one replays recorded PD finger motion, the other is commanded by the model or by WFLC; model set to predict 50 ms ahead to cover data-processing and motor delay
participants_or_bench: 18 PD participants (12 train, 3 validation, 3 test); IMUs on hand/wrist at 100 Hz; tasks include resting, pencil pinching/moving and spiral drawing; bench replay of all 18
key_quantitative_findings: Estimation accuracy (EPA) 99.2% (RMSE 0.000313 deg/s). Prediction accuracy (PPA) 97.0 / 94.0 / 91.7 / 90.6% at 10 / 20 / 50 / 100 steps = 100 / 200 / 500 / 1000 ms (abstract gives 91.6 / 89.9% for 50 / 100 steps); prediction time as low as 1.5 ms for 100 steps (desktop PC; i7-9700 CPU, RTX 2060 used for training). Bench tremor PSD reduction 93.8+/-1.5% (model) vs 68.8+/-7.5% (WFLC); voluntary-tracking RMSE 0.07 vs 3.7 deg/s; RMSE rose from 0.012 (simulation) to 0.12 deg/s (bench).
units_and_conditions: Joint angular velocity (deg/s); ground-truth voluntary motion = 2 Hz low-pass applied zero-phase offline, tremor = 3-17 Hz band; PPA = (1-|true-pred|/|true|)x100; motor-pair bench, not a hand or pen
locator: Abstract; Sec I (delay and prior-work claims); Sec III.A-C (data, preparation, metrics); Sec IV (Tables I-III); Sec V.A-C (Figs 8-17, 50 ms horizon, 1.5 ms prediction time)
limitations: Voluntary motion defined as <=2 Hz; PPA metric dominated by slow component; rotary bench without contact; model size not stated; inference timed on a desktop PC
relevance_to_design: Only learned predictor here compared in-loop with WFLC under an explicit ~50 ms delay budget
transferability_reason: Multi-step prediction to cover measured latency is exactly what a pen needs, but the <=2 Hz voluntary definition conflicts with handwriting content, signals are joint angular velocities not nib displacement, and compute is desktop-class
design_implication: Plan predictors with horizon >= measured loop delay; redefine ground truth for handwriting (voluntary strokes may overlap the tremor band); benchmark MCU-class inference latency and memory

topic: Commercial handheld active stabiliser: Liftware (Lift Labs) ACT spoon pilot in essential tremor
citation: Pathak A, Redmond JA, Allen M, Chou KL. A noninvasive handheld assistive device to accommodate essential tremor: a pilot study. Mov Disord. 2014;29(6):838-842.
task_or_setup: Active Cancellation of Tremor (ACT) handle: two DC motors with mechanical yokes move a detachable spoon in horizontal and vertical directions opposite to sensed tremor; tri-axial accelerometer 'embedded in the spoon base'; tasks holding, eating, transferring; device on vs off, randomised order, subject and neurologist blinded; accelerometer logged at 100 Hz, 12 bit
participants_or_bench: 15 ET (9 M, 6 F); accelerometer analysis in 11
key_quantitative_findings: Accelerometer tremor-amplitude reduction 72% (holding), 76% (eating), 71% (transferring); mean 73%. Change in Fahn-Tolosa-Marin TRS (on vs off): holding 1.00+/-0.76 vs 0.27+/-0.70 (P=0.016), eating 1.47+/-1.06 vs 0.13+/-0.64 (P=0.001), transferring 1.33+/-0.82 vs 0.27+/-0.59 (P=0.001); CGI-S improved for eating and transferring, not holding. Device ~100 g, 40x50x175 mm, >90 min battery. Actuator travel, bandwidth and latency not stated. Two subjects with severe tremor (DBS off) could not use the device.
units_and_conditions: Amplitude at the dominant frequency from double-integrated acceleration after 1st-order 2-25 Hz band-pass (measured by the device's own sensor); ET kinetic tremor; free space
locator: Abstract; Methods (ACT prototype, signal processing); Table 2 (change in TRS); Table 3 (accelerometer %)

transferability_reason: cm-scale travel in free space (see ACT-17) with spill-avoidance goals, versus +/-0.5 mm nib travel in frictional paper contact with trace-accuracy goals
design_implication: Expect severe tremor to saturate +/-0.5 mm travel and define the target population by tremor amplitude at the nib; reuse the blinded on/off design but with trace metrics and independent (not on-device) measurement

topic: Passive inertial/spring-isolated tremor pen: observed nib-paper contact behaviour
citation: Dessau PM. Writing pen for essential tremors patients. MS thesis, Mechanical Engineering, California State University, Sacramento; 2012 (committee chair A. Kumagai).
task_or_setup: Passive pen: weighted inner pen holder suspended by rubber-band springs inside an outer shell (shell ID 35 mm, OD 42.5 mm, length 147.5 mm; ~0.226 kg found best by trial); informal tests drawing horizontal, vertical and spiral lines vs regular, ergonomic and weighted pens, an earlier tremor pen and a drafting arm

Observations: 'The pen tip does not vibrate on the paper when the shell is vibrating when the inner assembly is weighted with 8 oz. or 0.2268 kg'; 'the inertia of the weight assembly combined with the static and dynamic friction of a standard ball point pen tip on the paper are the components that prevent the pen from shaking'; because the pen tip constrains the inner assembly it acts as a pivot and vibration was transferred to the top springs, adding vibration at the tip until top stiffness was increased; 'The pen tip encounters to [sic] most static friction during these maneuvers [curves] and tends to release, uncontrollably while negotiating the curve'; lighter pen pressure on small curves helped; ergonomic and weighted pens gave the most positive results; outcomes 'highly variable' and a learning curve was needed.
units_and_conditions: Qualitative user feedback forms; ballpoint on paper
locator: Abstract pp. iv-v; p. 6 (tip does not vibrate on paper with 8 oz inner assembly); p. 10 (shell dimensions); p. 12 (8 oz best; inertia plus nib-paper friction statement); p. 15 (tip acts as pivot); p. 16 (static friction, uncontrolled release on curves, learning curve); pp. 19-20 (participants, ergonomic/weighted pens best, lighter pressure)

topic: Actuator figure of merit and flexure safety factor (moving-magnet actuator + flexure)
citation: Hiemstra DB, Parmar G, Awtar S. Performance Tradeoffs Posed by Moving Magnet Actuators in Flexure-Based Nanopositioning. IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics (accepted-manuscript PDF).
task_or_setup: Lumped magnetostatic derivation of moving-magnet-actuator tradeoffs, then design, build and test of a single-axis flexure nanopositioner
participants_or_bench: Bench prototype: MMA plus double-parallelogram flexure bearing
comparator: Piezo stacks, quasi-static and ultrasonic piezomotors, voice-coil actuators (literature review in paper)
key_quantitative_findings: Actuator constant (force per sqrt(power)) is the traditional figure of merit. For traditional MMAs, force is proportional to sqrt(moving-magnet mass) x sqrt(power), which defines a 'dynamic actuator constant'. Flexure beams 0.75 x 25.4 x 80 mm give motion stiffness 3.43 N/mm and +/-5 mm stroke with a safety factor of 4 against yielding (natural frequency 25 Hz). The system achieved 10 mm range, 4 nm resolution and less than 0.5 degC temperature rise with a passive thermal-management system. Ultrasonic piezomotors reach 100-500 mm/s but under 10 N, and quasi-static and ultrasonic piezomotors have low fatigue life (cited).
locator: Abstract; Sec. II-A (actuator review); Sec. III (tradeoffs); flexure design and thermal-management sections (pp. 1-3, 8)
limitations: Macro-scale nanopositioner rather than pen scale; piezomotor statements are literature citations.
relevance_to_design: Supports ranking actuators by Km and moving mass, treating thermal management as first-order, and a flexure safety factor of about 4 on yield.
transferability_reason: The scaling laws transfer; geometry and thermal environment differ.
design_implication: Rank candidates by nib-referred Km and reflected moving mass; design flexures with safety factor 4 or more on yield (static), then check fatigue separately (see AMF-19, AMF-26).

topic: Flexure design guidance - allowable deflection vs yield and safety factor
citation: Awtar S. Synthesis and Analysis of Parallel Kinematic XY Flexure Mechanisms. PhD thesis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, February 2004.
task_or_setup: Beam-flexure design limits and material selection for an XY flexure stage
key_quantitative_findings: With the maximum-shear-stress yield criterion, max allowable tip displacement is Delta/L <= (1/(3*eta)) * (Sy/E) * (L/T), where eta is a safety factor chosen for stress concentration. L/T ratios of 50 are common. Sy/E ranges from 4e-3 (AL-6061) to 1e-2 (Ti). Typical max deformation is 0.05L-0.1L, but in practice it is kept well within this when fatigue loading is considered. Beryllium copper has an excellent Sy/E but was rejected for fabricability; AL6061-T651 was chosen for low internal stress.
units_and_conditions: Static yield criterion; fatigue treated qualitatively
locator: Sec. 3, eq. (3.2) (PDF p. 56); material selection (PDF p. 158)
limitations: Static yield basis; no numeric fatigue allowable; Smith (2000) and Howell (2001) texts were not accessed.
relevance_to_design: Gives the sizing relation linking flexure length and thickness to the +/-0.5 mm stroke at a chosen stress.
transferability_reason: Beam mechanics are scale-independent.
design_implication: Size flexure beams on the fatigue allowable (about 150 MPa for C17200 TH04) in place of Sy/eta. MY CALC example: a fixed-guided beam has sigma = 3*E*T*delta/L^2, so L >= sqrt(3*T*delta/alpha) with alpha = sigma/E = 150/127600 = 1.18e-3. For T = 0.1 mm and delta = 0.5 mm, L >= 11.3 mm; for T = 0.05 mm, L >= 8.0 mm.

topic: Touch-temperature limits - hazard-based ICT safety (precursor of IEC 62368-1)

topic: normal force (axial) - healthy adults
citation: Schomaker LRB, Plamondon R. The relation between pen force and pen-point kinematics in handwriting. Biological Cybernetics 63:277-289
task_or_setup: Cursive Dutch word 'gestaakt' (10 reps) plus drawing patterns (finger lines, wrist lines, CW/CCW circles 5-6 mm, scribbles), 12 s trials at normal pace; lab stylus with strain-gauge axial force transducer (0-10 N) holding a normal ballpoint refill, writing on A4 paper placed on a Calcomp 9000 tablet (105.2 Hz); forearm fixed in a cuff
participants_or_bench: 16 right-handed students (5 M, 11 F), mean age 23.3 y
comparator: Between patterns (cursive vs simple drawing) and between subjects
key_quantitative_findings: Axial pen force (APF) while writing the cursive word: per-subject means 57-212 g (0.56-2.08 N); mean of the 16 subject means 103 g = 1.01 N, between-subject SD 44 g = 0.43 N, median 96 g = 0.94 N (computed by CON from Table 4a); within-word SD 11-25 g (0.11-0.25 N), mean 18 g. Condition means (Table 2): scribbles 83.6 g, wrist lines 87.5 g, CW circles 108.9 g, cursive 109.7 g (variance 806 g^2, highest), finger lines 113.5 g, CCW circles 115.3 g. Within a trial (maximum 12 s; mean word duration 4.9 s) APF drifted +8 g/s in cursive (linear-fit start 91.6 g, end 127.7 g) and -1 to -2 g/s in drawing patterns. APF only weakly coupled to kinematics (coherence <0.5; mean r(APF, finger displacement) = -0.23).
units_and_conditions: grams-force along the pen axis (APF), not normal to the page (1 g = 9.81 mN); transducer low-pass 2nd-order Butterworth -3 dB at 17.5 Hz, 10-bit; paper on digitiser (hard underlay); forearm immobilised
locator: Methods 2.1-2.2; Results; Table 2 (preprint p.30) and Table 4a (p.31)
limitations: Forearm fixed in cuff (restricts natural writing); 16 young students; single word; hard underlay; axial rather than normal force; 1990 transducer; ballpoint type/ink not specified
relevance_to_design: Direct measure of the axial contact load the moving nib must carry during natural cursive writing with a ballpoint on paper
transferability_reason: Ballpoint refill on paper, adult writers, force measured at the refill exactly where our actuator sits; only posture restriction and underlay differ
design_implication: Use ~1.0 N nominal axial load, between-writer 0.5-2.1 N, within-word SD ~0.2 N and slow upward drift within words when sizing the nib support, actuator holding force and any force sensing
search_query: WebSearch: Schomaker Plamondon 1990 "relation between pen force and pen-point kinematics in handwriting"; curl https://www.ai.rug.nl/~lambert/papers/pen-pressure.pdf

topic: pen tilt angle; friction; force/kinematic spectra
citation: Schomaker LRB, Plamondon R. The relation between pen force and pen-point kinematics in handwriting. Biological Cybernetics 63:277-289 (angle, friction and spectral results)
task_or_setup: As CON-01; additional control recordings with a modified tablet controller giving pen angle (accuracy 3 deg), T = 9 s
comparator: Axial vs normal pen force; kinematic vs force spectra
key_quantitative_findings: Pen angle to the writing plane averaged about 50 deg with variation amplitude about 2.5 deg; correlation between axial and normal pen force never below 0.96; authors state orientation variations seldom exceed 10 deg in normal-size cursive (~2.5 mm high 'a'). Friction: cites Dooijes (1984) estimate that ballpoint friction is about 4% of normal pen force in the 0-2 N range. Spectra: all kinematic and dAPF power spectra peak at 2-5 Hz; scribbling peak 4.5 Hz, circling 3.5 Hz; dAPF has relatively more power above 8 Hz (attributed to friction hysteresis and paper irregularities). Authors quote 8-12 strokes/s for adult cursive.
units_and_conditions: Angle between pen long axis and writing plane (altitude); F_N = F_A x sin(angle); spectra of differentiated signals, resolution 0.103 Hz (patterns) / 0.411 Hz (words)
locator: Introduction pp.3-4; Results p.16 (pen-angle control); Results pp.14-15 (PSDFs); Discussion pp.21-22 (Dooijes friction estimate; strokes/s)
limitations: Angle result from only 4 subjects with fixed forearm; the 4% friction figure is a secondary citation of Dooijes (1984), not re-measured; strokes/s is a statement, not tabulated
relevance_to_design: Gives pen altitude for converting axial to normal/lateral load, shows tilt is nearly constant within writing, and flags that contact-force signals carry >8 Hz texture/friction content
transferability_reason: Same physical situation (ballpoint on paper, adults); angle sample small
design_implication: Model nib load with a fixed tilt of ~50-60 deg per writer; the lateral (perpendicular-to-axis) component of the contact force is then ~0.5-0.65 x normal force (cosine of tilt) plus or minus friction, and must be reacted by the actuator; contact-force sensing will see >8 Hz friction/texture noise

task_or_setup: PHANToM Omni stylus over a flat screen; Exp 1: 2 Arabic + 2 Japanese-inspired unfamiliar letters (20 test trials pre/post); Exp 2: ellipses, test shapes never trained. Three training sessions per participant (Latin square): position guidance HGP (PD spring pulling tip to the next trajectory point; 0.4 N/mm, 0.2 N.s/mm in Exp 1; 0.6 N/mm, 0.2 N.s/mm in Exp 2), force guidance HGF (expert force profile from a 0.1 kg model; PD 0.5 N/mm, 0.1 N.s/mm), no guidance NHG
participants_or_bench: Exp 1: 23 right-handed adults (18-26 y); Exp 2: 24 right-handed adults (18-28 y)
comparator: No-guidance training session; pre vs post tests without guidance in the same session
key_quantitative_findings: Exp 1: velocity-peak decrease only after HGF (session x period F(2,44) = 5.01, p < .05; e.g., letter 2: 9.42 -> 7.06 peaks; letter 4: 11.12 -> 8.86); mean velocity increased only after HGF (F(2,44) = 11.09, p < .05); no training effect on shape (DTW) for any mode (authors suggest ceiling effect). Exp 2 (untrained ellipses, mean +/- SE, Table 2): velocity peaks HGP 14.48 -> 10.19, HGF 14.19 -> 9.20 (both significant; NHG 11.36 -> 13.80), mode x test F(2,46) = 8.86; mean velocity HGF 4.62 -> 6.23 cm/s (significant; HGP 5.13 -> 5.88, NHG 5.66 -> 5.14), F(2,46) = 13.22; shape (DTW) no interaction, F(2,46) = 0.45.
units_and_conditions: Velocity peaks per trajectory, mean velocity (cm/s), DTW shape score; immediate post-test without guidance
locator: Methods (Exp 1 training sessions; Exp 2); Results Exp 1 (velocity peaks, mean velocity, shape matching) and Exp 2 with Table 2; Discussion
limitations: No delayed retention; three training sessions per participant (Latin square) with carry-over risk; adults; time-indexed playback guidance; stylus on a screen, not ink on paper
relevance_to_design: Handwriting-like evidence that guidance improves fluency (kinematics) but not shape, and that force-profile guidance beats position guidance
transferability_reason: Grounded device that moves the hand; the pen cannot apply net force to the hand, but the null effect of position correction on shape is directly relevant
design_implication: Do not expect nib correction to teach shape; if a cue for fluency is wanted, make it about timing/velocity (e.g., vibrotactile rhythm) rather than position

topic: 3 drawing guidance & position-correcting tools
citation: Korres G, Park W, Eid M (2021) Contactless kinesthetic feedback to support handwriting using magnetic force. IEEE Trans Haptics (accepted manuscript)
task_or_setup: KATIB: 2-DOF parallel manipulator moves a permanent magnet under a touchscreen; stylus carries stacked neodymium magnets. Proactive (full) guidance: magnet leads point-to-point at maximum force; retroactive (partial): magnet activated only when stylus-to-target distance exceeds epsilon. Psychophysics: copy task of unfamiliar Arabic letters (5 difficulty levels), kinesthetic feedback randomly on/off, 10 s target duration
key_quantitative_findings: Maximum lateral force 0.43 N at 3.5 mm magnet-stylus offset; stylus tilt up to 40 deg from normal gives negligible lateral force; workspace 80 x 60 mm; unattended playback RMSE < 3 mm; copy RMSE significantly lower with feedback at all difficulty levels (t-test, p < 0.01); completion time closer to the 10 s target with feedback; ergonomics rating mean 59 % (0-100).
units_and_conditions: N, mm, RMSE (mm), s; guided (assisted) performance only
limitations: No retention test; only proactive guidance tested; epsilon not reported in extracted text; adults
relevance_to_design: Tip-level forces of ~0.4 N suffice to steer a lightly held stylus; tilt sensitivity and workspace limits matter; users valued free stylus control
transferability_reason: Grounded magnetic force at the tip vs ungrounded nib displacement; force levels and acceptance data still informative
design_implication: Error-triggered (retroactive) help maps to a deadband correction; measure retention separately from assisted accuracy

citation: Langerak T, Zarate J, Vechev V, Panozzo D, Hilliges O (2019) Dynamic drawing guidance via electromagnetic haptic feedback. arXiv:1906.11753; peer-reviewed version: Langerak T, Zárate JJ, Vechev V, Lindlbauer D, Panozzo D, Hilliges O (2020) Optimal control for electromagnetic haptic guidance systems. Proc. UIST '20
task_or_setup: Electromagnet (Intertec ITS-MS-5030-12VDC, 5 cm dia., 12 V, 11 W) on a bi-axial stepper stage (full step 0.2 mm, quarter-stepped) under a Sensel Morph tablet (6502 DPI, 500 Hz, 2 ms latency); ordinary paper; 3D-printed ballpoint pen with ring magnet; time-free model-predictive contouring control (horizon N = 10) pulls the pen back toward the path while the user sets the speed; if the pen is lifted the last known position is used (UIST version)
participants_or_bench: Exp A: 12 participants (open loop dePENd-like vs time-indexed MPC vs MPCC, one complex shape); Exp B: 12 participants (8 M, 4 F, 28.2 +/- 2.2 y), 6 shapes each drawn once with and once without guidance
key_quantitative_findings: Lateral force up to 488 mN at 11 W; positional dispersion 2.8 +/- 0.8 mm (300 repetitions, magnet full strength, passive pen); solve time 7.4 +/- 3.0 ms, pen-to-magnet latency ~10 ms, ~20 ms total. Exp A pen-to-path error OL 4.1 +/- 0.7, MPC 3.9 +/- 1.3, MPCC 2.0 +/- 0.6 mm (H(2) = 20.76, p < .001); pen-to-magnet 38.2 +/- 25.1 / 8.6 +/- 1.6 / 4.6 +/- 0.9 mm. Corner cutting grows with curvature (simulation, Fig. 16). No learning/retention measured ('long-term learning ... beyond the scope').
units_and_conditions: mm (mean +/- SD), mN, ms, Likert 1-5; assisted performance
locator: arXiv v1: Sec. 4.1 p. 4; Secs. 6.3-6.4 p. 9; Sec. 7 and Table 2 pp. 9-10; Sec. 8 and Table 3 pp. 10-11; Table 4 p. 12; Secs. 10-11 p. 13; UIST'20 'Input and Output Devices'

transferability_reason: Tip forces from ground vs ungrounded nib displacement; the control concepts (time-free progress variable, gentle pull-back) transfer fully
design_implication: Parameterise the target by a time-free progress variable along the path; pull back smoothly rather than snap; accept that the nib can only polish, not form, novice shapes

citation: Rivers A, Moyer IE, Durand F (2012) Position-correcting tools for 2D digital fabrication. ACM Trans Graph 31(4) (Proc. SIGGRAPH 2012)
task_or_setup: Handheld frame (~13 x 10 x 9 in) carrying a router, vinyl cutter or pen; frame camera tracks printed marker tape (image registration ~4 ms); two stepper-driven eccentrics move the tool within the frame; on-tool screen shows plan, tool position and correction-range circle
participants_or_bench: Authors' prototype; no formal user study
comparator: Manual positioning (pilot: users with an accurate location display kept the tool within 1/8 in of the plan)
key_quantitative_findings: Correction range set to twice the observed human error: users stayed within 1/8 in (3.2 mm) -> range radius 1/4 in (6.35 mm; 1/2 in circle); stage limited to ~95 % of eccentric range; 62 oz-in steppers prevented backdriving. Constant-speed mode: tool advances at 0.2 in/s (~5 mm/s) by default and stops at the range edge until the user catches up. Freeform mode: target = closest plan point to the range centre; 4 ranked candidate paths (walk along the border within range ... 'don't move'); user should not diverge faster than ~0.2 in/s. Pen plot of a 6 in pattern: mean error 0.009 in (0.23 mm), max 0.023 in (0.58 mm).
units_and_conditions: inch values converted to mm; in/s; ms
locator: PDF pages: Sec. 3.4 p. 3; Secs. 4-4.1 pp. 3-4; Secs. 4.2.1-4.2.2 and Fig. 5 pp. 4-5; Sec. 5.1 and Fig. 6 p. 5; Sec. 6 and Fig. 10 p. 6
limitations: Bench demonstrations only; frame rests on the workpiece (effectively grounded, large); no learning or user-performance statistics
relevance_to_design: Closest architectural analogue: the human supplies coarse motion and the device corrects small errors within a bounded range, with explicit rules for range sizing and for leaving range
transferability_reason: Same division of labour and bounded correction; differences are range (+/-0.5 mm vs +/-6.35 mm) and a hand-held, ungrounded pen body
design_implication: Size range from measured user error; show or cue remaining headroom; when out of range hold/stop rather than jump, prefer staying on the path over shortcuts, and re-acquire when the user returns

topic: 4 shared control / virtual fixtures
citation: Abbott JJ, Marayong P, Okamura AM (2007) Haptic virtual fixtures for robot-assisted manipulation. In: Robotics Research (ISRR), Springer STAR 28:49-64; with Marayong P, Okamura AM (2004) Speed-accuracy characteristics of human-machine cooperative manipulation using virtual fixtures with variable admittance. Hum Factors 46(3):518-532 (abstract)
task_or_setup: Guidance and forbidden-region virtual fixtures on admittance-type (JHU Steady-Hand) and impedance-type telemanipulators; guidance level set by the admittance ratio (gain orthogonal to path / gain along path)
participants_or_bench: Steady-Hand experiments (N not stated in chapter); forbidden-region compliance study with 8 users (Fig. 7)
key_quantitative_findings: Path following was more accurate with guidance fixtures (significant) though not significantly faster; in off-path targeting and avoidance users took significantly longer with stronger guidance and error increased slightly; appropriate guidance is task dependent. Marayong & Okamura 2004: linear relation between admittance ratio and performance; algorithm to select the ratio by task; automatic tuning recommended. Li & Okamura (2003) used hidden Markov models to recognise user motions and switch assistance in combined curve-following/obstacle-avoidance. Impedance-type fixtures are stability-limited (Fig. 8). Open question whether fixtures can act as removable 'training wheels'.

limitations: Summary chapter; grounded devices; no learning outcomes; Marayong 2004 full text blocked
relevance_to_design: Quantifies the trade-off: stronger guidance helps on the path and hurts when the user means to leave it, motivating intent-dependent authority
transferability_reason: Guidance strength maps to nib correction gain; off-path costs map to intended deviations and letter branches
design_implication: Use a continuous correction gain (0-1, admittance-ratio-like) rather than on/off, and lower it when intent to leave the path or take another branch is detected

citation: Abbink DA, Carlson T, Mulder M, de Winter JCF, Aminravan F, Gibo TL, Boer ER (2018) A topology of shared control systems - finding common ground in diversity. IEEE Trans Hum-Mach Syst 48(5):509-525; with Abbink DA, Mulder M, Boer ER (2012) Haptic shared control: smoothly shifting control authority? Cogn Tech Work 14:19-28 (not retrieved) and Mulder M, Abbink DA, Boer ER (2012) Sharing control with haptics. Hum Factors 54(5):786-798 (abstract)
task_or_setup: Definition, design axioms and domain reviews (automotive, surgery, brain-machine interfaces, learning) of shared control; Mulder 2012: fixed-base driving-simulator curve negotiation, manual vs haptic shared control vs automation
key_quantitative_findings: Shared control: human and robot interact congruently in a perception-action cycle on a task either could do alone. Axiom 1: each agent directly perceives how its intent is shaped by the other; corollary: minimise conflicts by modelling robot actions on human behaviour and, in conflicts, ensure the human has time and ability to influence the robot. Level of haptic authority = stiffness around the controller's optimal steering angle (automotive example). Learning: fixed-gain guidance may be detrimental and shared control can de-skill; participants get annoyed when resisting forces contrary to their intentions. Mulder 2012 (abstract): vs manual, haptic shared control needed 16 % lower steering-wheel reversal rate and 15 % lower SD of wheel angle with 11 % lower peak lateral error; full automation gave 35 % lower peak lateral error but placed the human in a supervisory role.
locator: Abbink 2018 (UCL accepted-manuscript pagination) Secs. II.A-II.B (pp. 3-4), III.B (p. 6), VI and VI.A (pp. 9-10); Mulder 2012 abstract (PubMed 23156623)
limitations: Review; driving/surgery domains; Abbink 2012 text not accessed (Springer login); Mulder numbers from abstract
relevance_to_design: Vocabulary and rules for continuous authority sharing and override/conflict handling
transferability_reason: Principles are domain independent; torque-level sharing on a grounded interface differs from ungrounded nib displacement
design_implication: Expose correction authority as a continuous gain the user can feel and overrule; avoid sustained conflict by fading correction when the writer persistently deviates; keep the writer in the loop in learning mode

citation: Dragan AD, Srinivasa SS (2013) A policy-blending formalism for shared control. Int J Robot Res 32(7):790-805
task_or_setup: Teleoperated robot reaching/grasping among candidate goals; assistance blends user input with the policy for the predicted goal via arbitration alpha(confidence); confidence c = max(0, 1 - d/D), d = distance to predicted goal; timid mode (alpha rises with confidence, plateaus below full) vs aggressive mode (takes over beyond a threshold); tasks Easy/Hard x prediction Right/Wrong
participants_or_bench: 8 participants (4 M, 4 F), within-subjects, balanced Latin square
comparator: Timid vs aggressive arbitration; correct vs wrong prediction
key_quantitative_findings: Completion time: hard tasks +22.9 s (F(1,53) = 18.45, p < .001); wrong prediction +30.1 s (F(1,53) = 31.88, p < .001); aggressive mode +19.4 s overall (F(1,53) = 13.2, p = .001); aggressiveness x correctness F(1,53) = 36.28, p < .001 - when wrong, timid significantly better (t(15) = 7.09, p < .001) and aggressive+wrong worse than all other cells; on Hard&Right aggressive was faster for every user; preference correlated with time difference (r(30) = .66, p < .001); some users preferred timid despite a time cost.
locator: Sec. 3.2 (arbitration); Sec. 4.1 and Fig. 7 (pp. 797-798); Sec. 5.1 and Fig. 8 (p. 799)
limitations: N = 8; goal reaching, not path tracing; arbitration hand-tuned
relevance_to_design: Direct evidence for confidence-based authority; confident-but-wrong assistance is the dominant failure, as at letter junctions
transferability_reason: Arbitration principle transfers; task and interface differ
design_implication: Scale nib authority with intent confidence; at junctions, loop closures and stroke starts use a timid profile that never fully takes over until the stroke direction disambiguates; allow per-user tuning

topic: 5 hand impedance
citation: Hajian AZ, Howe RD (1997) Identification of the mechanical impedance at the human finger tip. J Biomech Eng 119(1):109-114
task_or_setup: Rapid force transients on the outstretched index fingertip (motion mainly at the MCP joint) in extension and abduction; second-order mass-spring-damper fit to ~20 ms of force/displacement data at mean fingertip forces 2-20 N (extension) and 2-8 N (abduction)
key_quantitative_findings: Effective translational fingertip mass roughly constant above 6 N in extension and constant in abduction; stiffness increased linearly with muscle activation; extension damping ratio ~1.7x abduction. Numeric m, b, k values not accessible (paywall) and not taken from unverified secondary sources.
units_and_conditions: Force 2-20 N; parameters in kg, N.s/m, N/m (values not extracted)
limitations: Abstract only; outstretched single finger, not a tripod pen grasp; short-transient (high-frequency, small-motion) regime
relevance_to_design: Stiffness scales with co-activation/force, so grip force must be a simulation parameter
transferability_reason: Single-finger MCP posture differs from pen grasp and no numbers were extracted
design_implication: Model hand stiffness as increasing with grip/co-contraction; obtain the paper's numeric values before using them

topic: 5 hand impedance
citation: Kuchenbecker KJ (2006) Characterizing and controlling the high-frequency dynamics of haptic interfaces. PhD thesis, Stanford University; with Kuchenbecker KJ, Park JG, Niemeyer G (2003) Characterizing the human wrist for improved haptic interaction. Proc. ASME IMECE 2003 (abstract)
task_or_setup: System identification of hand-held haptic devices: (a) custom 1-DOF stylus interface with grip-force sensor, swept sines 1-2000 Hz, grip 0-7 N; (b) force-feedback joystick (thesis Sec. 3.5 system) held in a comfortable grasp, 10-200 Hz sweeps; (c) 2003: wrist flexion/extension impedance while holding a stylus in a three-finger grasp
participants_or_bench: Single user(s) in thesis tests; 2003 study N not in abstract
comparator: Device alone (zero grip) vs held; grip-force levels
key_quantitative_findings: Holding the stylus adds a low-frequency spring and mid-frequency damper: response slope about +40 dB/decade below ~5 Hz and +20 dB/decade from ~5 to ~80 Hz; stiffness and damping rise with grip force (Fig. 3.12). Joystick user model: k_u = 40 N/m, b_u = 23 N.s/m with handle mass 0.014 kg (Table 3.1). Users actively compensate low-frequency induced motion from DC to about 8 Hz. 2003: positive linear correlation between grip force and wrist impedance for all subjects, with individual trends.
units_and_conditions: N/m, N.s/m, kg, Hz; grip force in N
locator: Thesis Sec. 3.4.6 and Fig. 3.12 (pp. 53-55); Sec. 3.5.2 'Handle and User Impedance' and Fig. 3.22 (p. 68); Table 3.1 (p. 73); Sec. 5.6.2 (pp. 136-137); 2003 IMECE abstract via search
limitations: Few users; joystick grasp is not a pen grasp; device-specific fits; 2003 numeric values not accessed
relevance_to_design: Frequency map of the user: active compensation below ~8 Hz, spring-like below ~5 Hz, damper-like ~5-80 Hz, mass-like above; grip force is the main modulator
transferability_reason: Stylus/handle grasps similar in kind; not a writing posture
design_implication: Simulate the writer as an active position controller below ~5-8 Hz plus a passive k-b-m load above; schedule k and b with grip force (consider a barrel grip-force sensor)

topic: 5 hand impedance
citation: Fu MJ, Cavusoglu MC (2012) Human-arm-and-hand-dynamic model with variability analyses for a stylus-based haptic interface. IEEE Trans Syst Man Cybern B Cybern 42(6):1633-1644
task_or_setup: Phantom Premium 1.5a with Nano17 force sensor; Delrin stylus (with gimbal 52 g) held 'as one would hold a pen'; elbow/arm unsupported; subject keeps a cursor static while random force (<= 5 N, coloured noise, 0.6-30 Hz) is applied along X (left-right), Y (up-down) or Z (fore-aft); grip force held at 1, 2 or 3 N. Model: stylus -(k1 || b1, grasp)- mass M -(k2 || b2, arm)- ground
comparator: Grip force 1/2/3 N; axes; inter-subject variability
units_and_conditions: kg, N/m, N.s/m; 0.6-30 Hz; grip 1-3 N; arm unsupported, static hold
locator: Author PDF pages: Secs. II.B-II.E, Fig. 4, Eq. 1 (pp. 2-5); Tables I-III (pp. 6-7); Sec. III.B (p. 7); Sec. IV (p. 8)

topic: 5 hand impedance + 6 perception thresholds
citation: Israr A, Choi S, Tan HZ (2006) Detection threshold and mechanical impedance of the hand in a pen-hold posture. Proc. IEEE/RSJ IROS 2006, 472-477
task_or_setup: B&K 4810 minishaker drives a PHANToM 1.0A stylus along its length (vibration mostly tangential to the skin); stylus held like a pen; elbow/forearm on an armrest; three-interval forced-choice adaptive thresholds (4 dB then 1 dB steps, 12 reversals) at 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 500 Hz; 1 s bursts; accelerometer and Nano17 force sensor
participants_or_bench: 10 participants (5 M, 5 F; 22-40 y); skin contact area 400-711 mm^2 (mean 550 mm^2)
comparator: Bolanowski et al. 1988 (thenar, normal indentation, surround) and Brisben et al. 1999 (grasped cylinder, tangential) as reported in the paper
key_quantitative_findings: Position thresholds 26 µm at 10 Hz and 8.5 µm at 20 Hz; mean slope -13 dB/octave from 10 to 160 Hz; minimum 0.06 µm at 320 Hz (vs 0.03 µm at 150 Hz in Brisben 1999; 0.13 µm at 300 Hz in Bolanowski 1988). Force thresholds U-shaped, minimum ~160 Hz. Skin impedance roughly constant below 40 Hz at -36 to -38 dB re 1 N.s/mm (about 12.6-15.8 N.s/m; conversion by this ledger), then -7 dB/octave (40-80 Hz) and -16 dB/octave (80-160 Hz), flat 160-320 Hz, +16 dB/octave 320-500 Hz. Prior haptic experience no effect (F(1,406) = 0.49, p = 0.48). Brisben 1999 abstract adds: contact force 0.05-1.0 N had no effect on grasped-cylinder thresholds.
units_and_conditions: Peak displacement (um); dB re 1 N.s/mm; axial excitation at threshold amplitudes
locator: PDF pages: Sec. II.A-C (pp. 2-3, Fig. 2); Sec. III (pp. 4-5, Figs. 3-5); Sec. IV (p. 5); Brisben: PubMed 10200190 abstract
limitations: Axial (along-barrel) excitation only; supported forearm; no writing; force-threshold values only graphical
relevance_to_design: Only data found on vibration detection and small-signal impedance in a pen-hold grasp
transferability_reason: Same grasp; in-plane nib reactions are partly off-axis from the tested direction
design_implication: Relative barrel-skin motion above ~26 µm at 10 Hz or ~8.5 µm at 20 Hz (far less near 160-320 Hz) is likely to be felt; keep actuator reaction spectra low and smooth or use them deliberately as cues; use ~13-16 N.s/m as a small-signal check

topic: 6 perception thresholds / force control
citation: Tan HZ, Srinivasan MA, Eberman B, Cheng B (1994) Human factors for the design of force-reflecting haptic interfaces. Proc. ASME Dynamic Systems and Control Division, DSC-Vol. 55-1, 353-359
task_or_setup: Summary of human capabilities for haptic interface design plus new measurements: pressure JND vs contact area, joint position resolution, maximum controllable force and force-control resolution at PIP, MCP, wrist, elbow and shoulder
key_quantitative_findings: Force JND ~7 % (Jones 1989; Pang et al. 1991 with 2.5-10 N references). Vibrotactile detection threshold ~28 dB re 1 µm (~25 µm) below 30 Hz, falling ~-12 dB/octave from 30 to 300 Hz (citing Bolanowski et al. 1988). Force-control bandwidth upper bound ~20-30 Hz (finger tremor peak ~25 Hz per Stiles & Randall 1967; ~20 Hz per Srinivasan & Chen 1993), actual ~7 Hz (Brooks 1990); vibration perceivable up to ~1000 Hz. Force-control resolution (SD while holding ~half-maximum force for 5 s with visual feedback) averaged 0.36 N (SD 0.07 N) at target forces 8.9-48.9 N (Table 4); maximum controllable force 16.5-102.3 N (Table 3).
limitations: Literature summary plus 3-subject tests; force control measured at forces far above writing forces; 28 dB threshold refers to normal indentation with a surround
relevance_to_design: Bounds what the writer can voluntarily correct (below ~7-20 Hz) versus what the pen must cancel, and how large force changes must be to be noticed
transferability_reason: General human limits; not measured in a writing posture or at writing forces
design_implication: Place cancellation above the writer's voluntary control band (~7 Hz) and leave lower frequencies to the writer; reaction-force changes above ~7 % of grip/contact force may be noticed

topic: 7 visual feedback in writing
citation: van Doorn RRA, Keuss PJG (1992) The role of vision in the temporal and spatial control of handwriting. Acta Psychol 81(3):269-286; van Doorn RRA, Keuss PJG (1993) Does the production of letter strokes in handwriting benefit from vision? Acta Psychol 82:275-290
task_or_setup: Adults writing nonsense letter sequences (e.g., 'lelele') with vs without vision
participants_or_bench: 1992: 12 subjects; 1993: adult writers (12 per Danna & Velay 2015 Table 1)
key_quantitative_findings: 1992: letter shapes remained equally invariant with and without vision (spatial control preserved) at the cost of longer processing time (reaction time increased without vision, more under short-duration instructions). 1993: without vision, movement time and trajectory size of stroke acceleration and deceleration phases increased, letter dependent ('l' more affected than 'e'), with increments spread across whole strokes.
units_and_conditions: RT, movement time, size; values not in abstracts
limitations: Abstracts only; skilled adults; vision removed rather than altered
relevance_to_design: Skilled writers form letter shapes largely without visual feedback; vision regulates size, spacing and timing
transferability_reason: Informs what writers rely on when the visible trace is altered, but no study altered the trace relative to the hand
design_implication: Expect skilled writers to keep their own shapes despite correction, so correction mainly affects fine appearance; whether writers notice or fight sub-mm corrections is untested
search_query: Europe PMC TITLE:"role of vision in the temporal and spatial control of handwriting" | TITLE:"production of letter strokes in handwriting benefit from vision"

topic: 7 visual feedback in writing
citation: Danna J, Velay J-L (2015) Basic and supplementary sensory feedback in handwriting. Front Psychol 6:169
task_or_setup: Review of natural (visual, proprioceptive, tactile) and supplementary (visual, haptic, auditory) feedback in handwriting control and learning
comparator: Vision vs no vision; delayed vision; supplementary feedback modalities
key_quantitative_findings: Vision mainly serves topocinetic (layout) control and stroke-repetition monitoring. Tamada (1995), 8 adults: visual-feedback delays of 0, 33, 67, 100, 133, 167, 267 and 500 ms increased writing error rate with delay, especially stroke repetitions (e.g., 'feeeling'). Smyth & Silvers (1987), 12 adults: word orientation affected by loss of vision. Supplementary concurrent visual feedback slows and disrupts fluency (Portier & van Galen 1992), so visual feedback should come after, not during, movement. Haptic guidance needs an a-priori 'ideal' trajectory, questionable given individual handwriting variability; auditory feedback recommended for real-time kinematics.
units_and_conditions: Delays in ms; error rates not reported in the review text
locator: Sections on visual feedback and Table 1; 'Supplementary proprioceptive FB' (haptic guidance); 'Supplementary auditory FB'
limitations: Narrative review; Tamada 1995 and Smyth & Silvers 1987 not accessed directly; no study displaces ink relative to the hand
relevance_to_design: Writers' visual loop is slow and supervisory; concurrent visual changes can disturb fluency
transferability_reason: Concerns the same visual trace the nib alters, but not the specific hand-vs-ink offset the pen creates
design_implication: Keep corrections small and smooth; in learning mode give error information after the stroke or through audio/vibration rather than concurrent visual changes; do not rely on a single 'ideal' template for all writers

topic: Pen-tip optical flow: DeltaPen hardware and pipeline
citation: Lüthi G., Fender A.R., Holz C. (2022). DeltaPen: A Device with Integrated High-Precision Translation and Rotation Sensing on Passive Surfaces. UIST '22, ACM, 12 pp.
task_or_setup: Prototype pen: two adjacent lens-less optical flow sensors on a tip PCB (rotated apart to maximise optical-centre separation), 3-axis accelerometer + magnetometer (InvenSense MPU9250 incl. AK8963; gyroscope unused), 8 mm FSR on the tip, wide-band LRA haptics; all fusion on a Teensy 4.0 (ARM Cortex-M7, 600 MHz); yaw from the difference of the two flow vectors.
participants_or_bench: Single prototype; engineering description and authors' operating-range observations
comparator: PixArt PMW3360 lens-based mouse sensor (datasheet comparison in text)
key_quantitative_findings: Sensors: 2x PixArt P3040 (lens-less), each reporting motion at 1000 Hz with NOMINAL resolution 6000 dpi (= 4.23 um/count, derived). P3040 tracks up to 200 mm from the surface but 'increasingly unreliably above a distance of 60 mm'; trackable surface typically detected within 20 mm; clutch by lifting ~2 cm. Tip PCB 10 mm x 12 mm; pen 190 mm long, 15 mm diameter. Both sensors on one 3-wire SPI bus. Accelerometer logged at 200 Hz, magnetometer at 100 Hz; FSR sampled at 200 Hz (13-bit ADC). Raw-flow outliers ~0.05% of samples (rejected by thresholding). Rotation: d_alpha = arcsin( s x (s+o) / (|s|*|s+o|) ), s = vector between optical centres, o = difference of the two sensors' motion vectors; tilt ('DPI') correction dx = x_raw/cos(theta), dy = y_raw/cos(psi) from the gravity vector; tip-offset compensation. End-to-end latency stated only as 'comparable to the latency of a tethered computer mouse' (no number). Sensor baseline |s| NOT reported numerically (bounded by the 10 x 12 mm PCB; diagonal 15.6 mm, derived). No numeric tilt limits reported.
units_and_conditions: Tethered: USB supplies power and data; processing on-pen; host receives processed motion; HID-mouse mode available.
locator: Sec. 3.1 Hardware (p.4) + Fig. 2; Sec. 3.2 Embedded processing + Fig. 3 (p.5); Sec. 3.3 Steps 1-7 (pp.5-6); Sec. 6 Limitations; Acknowledgments (PixArt provided the sensors)
limitations: Latency, sensor baseline and usable tilt range not quantified; no public P3040 datasheet found (sensors supplied by PixArt); tethered; gyroscope unused; absolute initial yaw needs a calibration step (Sec. 6).
relevance_to_design: Closest published precedent for pen-tip, lens-less, 1 kHz relative motion sensing that leaves room for a real ballpoint tip - the local paper-relative measurement the stabiliser needs.
transferability_reason: Same form factor (pen with real tip) and measurand (motion relative to the surface); differences are the actuated nib, paper vs tablet surface and an untethered power budget.
design_implication: Use dual lens-less flow sensors + IMU as the reference architecture for the research pen; request P3040 (or successor) samples and datasheet from PixArt early; keep the actuated nib out of the sensors' field of view; measure latency explicitly because DeltaPen does not report it.
search_query: https://static.siplab.org/papers/uist2022-deltapen.pdf

topic: Pen-tip optical flow: DeltaPen measured accuracy and drift
citation: Lüthi G., Fender A.R., Holz C. (2022). DeltaPen (UIST '22), technical evaluation (Sec. 4).
task_or_setup: DeltaPen rigidly coupled tip-to-tip to a Wacom pen on a Wacom Intuos 4; tasks: small (2-4 cm) and large (~10 cm) shapes for 1 min each, 5 sentences in block and cursive, ~5 min free sketch, shapes while hovering; offline comparison of pipeline variants with a GLMM.
participants_or_bench: 10 participants (4 female), aged 25-31 (mean 26.7); 209,986 data points after cleaning
comparator: Translation: deltas of Wacom Intuos 4 absolute positions; yaw: OptiTrack (3 IR cameras)
key_quantitative_findings: MEASURED translation error (magnitude, per 10 ms window): MAE 0.0683 mm, median 0.0236 mm (MAE ~16 counts of the 6000 dpi nominal resolution, derived). Yaw error per 40 ms window (rad): unprocessed median 5.25e-3 / mean 9.56e-3; with magnetometer damping median 4.75e-3 (0.27 deg) / mean 9.19e-3 (0.53 deg); tilt 'DPI correction' made yaw error worse (median 5.60e-3). Accumulated angular drift 0.160e-2 rad/s (0.092 deg/s) over all samples. Idle drift: yaw 9.07e-5 rad/s; translation 0.04375 mm/s in each of X and Y (= 2.6 mm/min, derived). Relative translation error (MdAPE) decreases with speed; Y error consistently larger than X; top velocity bin >= 11.875 cm/s.
units_and_conditions: Surface = Wacom Intuos 4 (not paper); samples within ~1 cm of the surface with clear OptiTrack view; X/Y errors computed after compensating absolute rotation; desk/table use shown only qualitatively.
locator: Sec. 4.1-4.4; Table 1 (p.7); Fig. 6-7 and paragraphs 'Angular drift', 'Idle Drift', 'Translation errors' (p.8)
limitations: No paper surfaces, no tilt sweep and no latency measurement; per-window errors are not stroke-level position errors; small young sample; Wacom ground truth has its own error; evaluated by the device's developers.
relevance_to_design: Only published measured accuracy/drift for a lens-less pen-tip flow pen; sets expectations for relative-motion quality available to the tremor controller and to stroke capture.
transferability_reason: Measured on a tablet surface with the pen coupled to a Wacom stylus; paper texture, ink trails and nib actuation can change flow quality.
design_implication: Budget ~0.07 mm MAE per 10 ms and ~2.6 mm/min idle translation drift for relative sensing; adequate for short-horizon stabilisation but page-level capture needs absolute re-anchoring; replicate this protocol on paper types with a tilt sweep and a latency measurement.
search_query: https://static.siplab.org/papers/uist2022-deltapen.pdf

topic: Pen-tip optical flow: Flashpen (PMW3360 in a pen tip)
citation: Romat H., Fender A., Meier M., Holz C. (2021). Flashpen: A High-Fidelity and High-Precision Multi-Surface Pen for Virtual Reality. IEEE VR 2021, pp. 306-315.
task_or_setup: Pen with a PixArt PMW3360 gaming-mouse sensor at the tip (lens and cover sanded down; flat tip on a cut LEGO hinge with 110 deg range), MPU6500 IMU and ESP32 tethered to a PC; flow sensor used on-surface, 2 OptiTrack Flex13 cameras give hover position and absolute yaw; tracing and writing blocks vs a Wacom pen.
comparator: Wacom professional drawing tablet pen; ordinary pen on paper (writing block)
key_quantitative_findings: Sensor run at 8,000 fps in burst mode; NOMINAL motion resolution stated as 1/226 mm (4.42 um); authors compare with ~200 Hz tablet digitisers. MEASURED tracing accuracy (mean shortest distance to reference normalised by shape width of 1/2/3 cm): ACCURATE instruction Flashpen 0.028 vs Wacom 0.026; FAST instruction 0.076 vs 0.079; no device x speed interaction (F1,9 = 0.80, p = 0.393). Pen mass ~200 g. Authors: works on 'most surface types (wood, paper, plastic and many more)', not glass.
units_and_conditions: Absolute yaw from cameras throughout (flow alone cannot give page orientation); tethered; Oculus Quest 2 via Link.
locator: Abstract; Sec. 3.1-3.2 (pp.3-4), Fig. 2-3; Sec. 5.1 (Block 1 results); Sec. 7 Limitations
limitations: Flat mouse-like contact tip, not a ballpoint; relies on external cameras for yaw and hover; writing block weaker than tracing; surface list qualitative; heavy prototype.
relevance_to_design: Shows a lens-based gaming sensor reaches tablet-like tracing fidelity at 8 kHz - but only with a flat contact tip at fixed height and an external yaw reference.
transferability_reason: Same sensor class; tip geometry and dependence on external tracking differ from a stand-alone ballpoint stabiliser.
design_implication: Use PMW33xx-class sensors on the bench rig (fixed Z) as the high-rate reference; in a ballpoint pen they need custom optics or a lens-less part; provide yaw from a second flow sensor or IMU/magnetometer rather than assuming it.

topic: Optical navigation sensors: PMW3360 / PMW3389 (lens-based, contact height)
citation: PixArt Imaging Inc. PMW3360DM-T2QU Product Datasheet, Version 1.30 (6 Apr 2016); PixArt Imaging Inc. PMW3389DM-T3QU Product Datasheet, Version 1.01 (3 Jan 2019, doc 11020AENW).
task_or_setup: Gaming-mouse navigation sensors with integrated IR illumination, 16-pin DIP, designed for the LM19-LSI 1:1 lens; 4-wire SPI.
participants_or_bench: Manufacturer characterisation on PixArt standard gaming surfaces (QCK, Vespula, FUNC 1030 etc.)
key_quantitative_findings: PMW3360: frame rate up to 12,000 fps (83 us/frame, derived); NOMINAL resolution up to 12,000 cpi in 100 cpi steps (2.1 um/count, derived); resolution error 1% typ (up to 200 ips on QCK at 5000 cpi); speed 250 ips typ; acceleration 50 g max; lens reference plane to surface Z = 2.2 / 2.4 / 2.6 mm (min/typ/max); lift detection 2 mm or 3 mm, or manual lift-cut-off calibration; SPI clock <= 2 MHz; burst-mode address-to-data delay tSRAD_MOTBR = 35 us (so a 6-byte motion burst takes ~59 us at 2 MHz, derived); SROM download registers (firmware upload at start-up). PMW3389: up to 16,000 cpi (50 cpi steps), 400 ips typ, 50 g, Z 2.2-2.6 mm, lift cut-off 2 or 3 mm, run current 21 mA incl. LED at VDD 1.9 V, package 10.90 x 16.20 x 5.01 mm, self-adjusting frame rate (maximum not in key parameters). Both datasheets plot mean resolution and path error versus Z (about 2.0-2.9 mm), i.e. the count scale depends on height.
units_and_conditions: Z plots: straight 4-inch line at 45 deg, 6 ips, 5000 cpi, on gaming mats; no paper, no tilt data.
locator: PMW3360 v1.30: p.1 Key Parameters; operating-conditions table (Z, speed, ResErr, acceleration); AC timing table (tSRAD_MOTBR); Fig. 12-13 (p.17). PMW3389 v1.01: p.1 Key Parameters; operating-conditions table (Z, lift cut-off); Fig. 11-12
limitations: Gaming-mat characterisation at fixed Z; +/-0.2 mm Z tolerance is incompatible with a tilting pen without redesigned optics; documents obtained from distributor mirrors.
relevance_to_design: Highest-rate, lowest-latency commodity motion sensors; ideal as the bench-rig reference channel over paper at controlled height.
transferability_reason: Electrical and timing data transfer directly; optical geometry (2.4 mm Z, flat contact) does not fit a tilted ballpoint tip.
design_implication: Put a PMW3360/3389 on a fixed-height carriage in the bench rig (8-12 kHz frames, ~0.1 ms read latency); do not base the product on them unless custom optics hold Z within +/-0.2 mm across tilt.
